newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House ethics report back on track.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House ethics report back on track.

text.p: House Republican leaders reversed course Wednesday and will proceed with a report by an ethics task force formed in the wake of Speaker Newt Gingrich's ethics troubles.

Democrats on the task force said they were told Tuesday night that the House Republican leadership had pulled the plug on the ethics report, which contained recommendations for improving procedures to review ethics complaints in the House.

Representative Benjamin Cardin of Maryland who was the Democratic co-chair of the task force spoke at what was originally scheduled as a bipartisan news conference to issue the ethics report, but turned into a Democrats-only appearance.

A spokeswoman for the Republican co-chair of the task force, Representative Bob Livingston of Louisiana, said there had been a procedural "glitch," but the problems were resolved and action on the report would proceed as soon as possible.
Cardin's spokeswoman later said he was "pleased the process is back on track."
Gingrich in December admitted he brought discredit to the House and was fined $300,000.
The ethics task force was formed in February to look at revamping House ethics procedures and there was a simultaneous moratorium on filing ethics complaints, due to be lifted soon.

The bipartisan ethics task force voted 11-1 Tuesday to approve the report recommending reform of House rules. The intention was to hold a public hearing on the report at the end of this week and then send the recommendations to the House floor for a vote early next week.
However, about 10 p.m. EST Tuesday, Cardin said he was called by Livingston who told him the task force was being disbanded and the report would not go forward.

"Last night I received a phone call from Bob Livingston ...advising me that the plug had been pulled and that the task force was out of existence and that there would not be any report that would be acted upon by the Congress," Cardin said, adding that Livingston was not to blame.

Christina Martin, spokeswoman for Gingrich, said bipartisan hearings on the ethics report would start after the July Fourth recess and that Gingrich had only been trying to slow down the process at the request of other House members.
"The Speaker was acting on behalf of a number of members who wanted to slow the process down and wanted time to be fully briefed," Martin said.

Representative David Hobson, an Ohio Republican, was one of the members asking for more time. "I raised a question about the material that I was shown," Hobson said. "I think the process will go forward, there was no intention to deep six it."

The report recommended the minority party's senior member on the House ethics committee have equal opportunity to put matters on the committee's agenda, that citizen complaints could not be filed exclusively based on newspaper articles, and provisions for "timely" resolution of ethics complaints.

"This is a corrupt politician's protection act because it would shield (congressional) members from scrutiny by the ethics committee," said Gary Ruskin, director of the Congressional Accountability Project, a watchdog group affiliated with consumer advocate Ralph Nader.
The proposed rule changes would make it more difficult for citizens to initiate complaints against a member of Congress, Ruskin said.
